1030.title: The Hajj by air
1030.hook: steamships then planes turn the long road to Mecca into days
1030.howItsDone: Pilgrims today usually fly to Saudi Arabia for Hajj, often arriving through Jeddah or Medina, and then perform the rites in and around Mecca on foot and by bus, wearing the same simple white garments.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Malcolm X at Hajj, writing home about pilgrims of every color sharing one plate. Your line was every color, one row. Today, how all those pilgrims got there.

At the airport in Jeddah there is a terminal built for one purpose. Its roof is a field of white peaks, like a great camp of tents, and under it, in the season of Hajj, planes unload pilgrims in white cloth from every corner of the world. Some flew overnight. Some changed planes twice. A grandmother from Dhaka, a nurse from Lagos, a retired teacher from Ohio, all walking out into the heat a day after leaving home. Their great-grandparents, if they went at all, went by camel, by foot, by ship. Today: the Hajj by air.
screen: `A ROOF LIKE A FIELD OF TENTS.` → `PILGRIMS FROM EVERY CORNER.` → `A DAY AFTER LEAVING HOME.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an calls people to the pilgrimage and pictures how they will come: "They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine." For a long time, that's how it was. Caravans crossed deserts from Cairo and Damascus. Travelers walked a long way, and some never came home; tradition remembers the road as part of the worship. Then the road changed. Steamships began carrying pilgrims across the Indian Ocean from India and Java to the port of Jeddah, crowded and often dangerous, but faster. Later came the airplane, and the long road shrank to a flight. Here's the turn worth noticing. The Qur'an makes Hajj a duty "for him who can find a way thither." Planes widened that way. A pilgrimage that could once take the work of a lifetime became something a nurse in Lagos could save for and do in her annual leave. And yet the rites themselves didn't shrink. Once they arrive, pilgrims still walk around the Ka'ba, still go between the hills, still stand at Arafat, still sleep under the sky at Muzdalifah. The plane gets you to the gate; the circling and the walk between the hills are still done step by step. Days, not years, to arrive; but the same days, once you're there, as every pilgrim before.

segments.voice: Think of someone who made a long journey for their faith, any faith: a grandparent who went on Hajj, a friend who drives two hours to a church, temple or gurdwara. Picture their bags, their tired feet, the moment they arrived, and then the pilots, cooks, drivers and families at home who made it possible. Hold each one for a breath and silently thank them, and if you pray, pray for travelers in your own way.
Jeddah, the Saudi port and airport city where Hajj pilgrims now land after ships and planes shortened the ancient road to Mecca. Today's word.
Your line: days, not years. Every road to Mecca was once a long one. Safe travels until tomorrow.

1031.title: The recited Qur'an on radio
1031.hook: reciters like Abdul Basit reach millions by radio and records
1031.howItsDone: Muslims listen to recorded recitation at home, in cars and in shops, and Qur'an radio stations broadcast it through the day; listeners often fall quiet while it plays, following the verse that asks them to give ear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hajj by air, ships and then planes carrying pilgrims to Jeddah. Your line was days, not years. Today, something else that started to travel fast.

A radio sits on a café shelf in a Cairo side street, turned low. A voice comes out of it, and the man wiping tables stops. The voice climbs, holds one note for what feels like a full breath and then some, and comes down again on the last word of a verse. Somebody in the back murmurs Allah under their breath. The same voice is coming out of a market stall in Karachi, a cassette player in a kitchen in Jakarta, a record player in Detroit. One man, reciting. Today: the recited Qur'an on radio.
screen: `A RADIO ON A CAFÉ SHELF.` → `ONE NOTE, HELD.` → `CAIRO, KARACHI, JAKARTA, DETROIT.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an asks to be heard: "And when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy." It also tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to "chant the Qur'an in measure." For a long time, that meant one reciter and the people within earshot. A great voice could fill a mosque, but no further. Then came the radio and the record. In Egypt, reciters were broadcast, and one of them, Sheikh Abdul Basit Abd us-Samad, became a voice that traveled far beyond Egypt. Fans describe how long he could hold a breath, and his recitations travel still, on old records, cassettes and now phones. People hear two broad styles. One is slow and ornate, with long held notes, the kind that makes a whole room go quiet. The other is plainer and steadier, good for following along or learning by heart. Both follow the careful rules of tajwid, which govern how each letter and pause is sounded. A hadith in Abu Dawud tells believers to beautify the Qur'an with their voices. Radio didn't change the words. It changed who could hear them: a farmer, a factory worker, a child in a city far from Cairo, all listening to the same voice at the same hour. One voice, millions.

segments.voice: If you can, play a short recording of Abdul Basit, perhaps al-Fatiha, the Qur'an's opening chapter, or simply remember any recitation you've heard. Don't try to understand every word; listen the way the verse asks, give ear and pay heed, and notice where his voice rises, where it holds, where it lets go. Notice your own breath while he holds his.
Tajwid, the careful rules for sounding each letter and pause of the Qur'an, that reciters like Abdul Basit followed as radio carried their voices worldwide. Today's word.
Your line: one voice, millions. The words stayed; only the reach grew. Day one thousand thirty-one.

1032.title: Women scholars, then and now
1032.hook: from Aisha to modern teachers of hadith and law
1032.howItsDone: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an, hadith and law in mosques, seminaries and universities, and communities often have women teachers who lead study circles for women and sometimes for mixed classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the recited Qur'an on radio, the voice of Abdul Basit keeping tajwid's rules in cafés, kitchens and market stalls. Your line was one voice, millions.

A group of women come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint. The men, they say, have taken all your time. Give us a day of our own. And he does. He sets a day, goes to them, and teaches them. That small scene sits in the Book of Knowledge in Sahih al-Bukhari. It's easy to miss. But it opens a long door: women asking for knowledge, getting it, and handing it on. Today: women scholars.
screen: `GIVE US A DAY OF OUR OWN.` → `HE SETS A DAY AND TEACHES THEM.` → `A LONG DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Start with Aisha, the Prophet's wife. Hadith after hadith comes through her: how he prayed, how he lived at home, what he said in private. Companions brought her their questions, and when she thought someone had reported the Prophet wrongly, she said so. Later scholars collected her corrections into a book of their own. Then follow the line forward. Women learned hadith from their fathers and teachers, memorized long chains of narrators, and taught men as well as women. One name worth knowing is Karima al-Marwaziyya, remembered for teaching Bukhari's great collection to students in Mecca; scholars traveled to hear it from her. In our own time, the scholar Mohammad Akram Nadwi set out to gather the names and lives of women hadith scholars, in a study called al-Muhaddithat, the women who narrate hadith. The Qur'an speaks to women and men side by side, line after line: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe." Today women teach hadith, law and Qur'an in mosques, seminaries and universities across the Muslim world and beyond. Schools and communities still differ on some questions about women's roles in leading prayer or giving rulings, and those debates are real. But on the simple question of whether women taught the faith, the record answers plainly: from Aisha's room onward, they did.

segments.voice: Say the first name quietly, Aisha, and breathe; then the second, Karima, and breathe. If you pray, ask God's mercy for each of them.
Women scholars. From Aisha and Karima to teachers today, women who learned the faith deeply and handed it on. Today's word.
Your line: they always taught. Every name you learn joins a very long list. Until tomorrow, then.

1033.title: The suffering ummah
1033.hook: wars, refugees and persecution today, and Muslim charities working amid them
1033.howItsDone: Muslims give zakat and voluntary charity, often through mosques and Muslim relief organizations that send food, medicine and shelter to people affected by war and disaster, and appeals are common at Friday prayers and in Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: women scholars, from Aisha correcting the reporters to Karima teaching Bukhari in Mecca. Your line was they always taught. Today is a harder one.

Rice, lentils, oil, a blanket, soap, a small bag of dates. Volunteers in mismatched gloves are packing them into boxes in a borrowed warehouse. Someone tapes, someone labels, someone's phone keeps buzzing with news from a place most of them have never seen. The boxes are going to people who left home with what they could carry. Nobody in the warehouse can stop the war that sent them running. They can fill the next box. Today: the suffering ummah.
screen: `RICE, OIL, A BLANKET, DATES.` → `A BORROWED WAREHOUSE.` → `THEY CAN FILL THE NEXT BOX.`

segments.voice: Ummah is the word for the community of believers, all Muslims everywhere, across every border. And in our time, parts of that body are hurting badly: war, displacement, refugee camps, persecution for faith or ethnicity. This lesson won't take sides in any conflict or rank anyone's pain. It looks at one teaching, and what people do with it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave a picture of how believers belong to one another. It is reported in Sahih Muslim: the believers, in their love and mercy and kindness to one another, are like one body. When one part of it aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Not sympathy from a distance. Fever. That's why news from one corner of the world can keep someone awake on the other side of it. And the picture asks for more than feeling. Across the Muslim world and in Muslim communities elsewhere, it has been turned into work: zakat committees, mosque food drives, large charities that run clinics, wells and shelters in war zones and after disasters, often alongside the Red Crescent and many others. Some of these charities say they help anyone in need, whatever their faith. The Qur'an puts the instruction plainly: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty." The body feels the pain. Then it does the next small thing.

segments.voice: Bring to mind people who have had to leave home, a family on a road, a child in a camp, someone waiting at a border, and don't picture anyone you can't bear to; keep it gentle. With each out-breath, hold one of them for a moment. If you pray, ask God's mercy for them in your own words; if not, simply hold them as you breathe.
Ummah, the worldwide community of believers that the Prophet pictured as one body, feeling fever when any part of it aches. Today's word.
Your line: the body feels the pain. Feeling it is where care begins. Be gentle with yourself today.

1034.title: About two billion
1034.hook: a number too big to picture, and the prayer rows behind it
1034.howItsDone: Muslims around the world pray at set times through the day, facing the Ka'ba in Mecca, so the times of prayer move across the globe with the sun.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the suffering ummah, believers like one body, answering pain with fever and then with work. Your line was the body feels the pain.

Dawn is moving across the earth right now, a thin gray line sliding west. Wherever it passes, somebody's alarm goes off, somebody washes in cold water, somebody unrolls a mat and stands to pray the dawn prayer. In Jakarta it happened hours ago. In Dhaka a little later. Then Karachi, then Cairo, then on toward the Atlantic and across it. As the earth turns, the call to prayer moves with it, like a wave that never quite reaches the shore. Today: about two billion.
screen: `DAWN SLIDES WEST.` → `JAKARTA, DHAKA, KARACHI, CAIRO.` → `A WAVE OF PRAYER AROUND THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: The title is an estimate, and so is today's line. Researchers who study populations put the number of Muslims in the world at about two billion, roughly a quarter of humanity. Counts differ, and no census can see into anyone's heart, so hold the number loosely. What matters more is what it's made of. Two billion is not a crowd. It's one person, then another, then another: a rice farmer in Java, a shopkeeper in Dakar, a midwife in Kazan, a student in Sarajevo, each with their own family, their own questions, their own way of keeping the faith. They speak a great range of languages. They follow different schools of law and different customs. They argue. Still, at the times of prayer they turn the same way, toward the Ka'ba in Mecca, and say the same opening chapter in the same Arabic. The Qur'an speaks to that scattered unity: "And each one hath a goal toward which he turneth; so vie with one another in good works. Wheresoever ye may be, Allah will bring you all together." These last weeks walked through the modern centuries: colonial rule, the last Mughal, the reformers, Iqbal, the caliphate's end, Partition, independence, enslaved Africans, Britain and America, radio, women scholars, and pain. That whole story ends here, in one huge number made of single faces.
screen: `AN ESTIMATE, HELD LOOSELY.` · `ONE PERSON, THEN ANOTHER.` · `MANY LANGUAGES, ONE DIRECTION.` · `WHERESOEVER YE MAY BE.` · then, large: `A QUARTER OF HUMANITY.`

segments.voice: Start with one prayer row you can see clearly, a mosque you know or one from a photo, then let it widen: a rooftop in Cairo, a school gym in Toronto, a ship's deck, a refugee camp, one person praying alone in an office stairwell. Don't count them; let them come one at a time, all turned toward the same center. If you pray, you can join them in your own way.
Ka'ba, the house in Mecca that roughly two billion Muslims worldwide turn toward at every prayer. Today's word, and the end of the modern centuries.
Your line: a quarter of humanity. Behind the number, a name, a kitchen, a morning. Day one thousand thirty-four, done.

1035.title: The Sacred Mosque
1035.hook: the mosque around the Ka'ba in Mecca
1035.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in the Sacred Mosque in Mecca for every prayer, using a mosque's prayer niche, a compass or a qibla app to find the direction, and pilgrims circle the Ka'ba within its courtyard during Hajj and Umrah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: about two billion, an estimate made of single faces, all turning toward one center, the Ka'ba. Your line was a quarter of humanity. Today, that center itself, and a new stretch of the path: houses of prayer.

Somewhere in the house there's a phone with a little compass app, or a sticker on a hotel ceiling with an arrow, or a grandmother who just knows: that way. Every one of those arrows points to the same place. Follow any of them far enough, over oceans and deserts, and you arrive at a great open courtyard in Mecca, white marble underfoot, colonnades all around, and in the middle a cube draped in black cloth, with crowds circling it day and night. The building around that cube has a name. Today's word: Masjid al-Haram.
screen: `A COMPASS APP, A CEILING ARROW.` → `ALL POINTING ONE WAY.` → `A COURTYARD IN MECCA.`

segments.voice: Masjid al-Haram means the Sacred Mosque: the mosque around the Ka'ba. Pickthall renders it the Inviolable Place of Worship, a place set apart, where fighting is forbidden and pilgrims come in peace. The Qur'an gives it a striking title: "Lo! the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind was that at Becca, a blessed place, a guidance to the peoples." Becca is understood as Mecca. The Qur'an also tells how Abraham and his son Ishmael raised the foundations of the House, and prayed that God accept it from them. Then a turning point. For a time in Medina, the reports say, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his companions prayed facing Jerusalem. Then a verse came: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." From that day, it has been the qibla, the direction of prayer, for Muslims everywhere: from a mosque in Senegal to a hospital prayer room in Seattle to a hiker on a mountain with a compass. A hadith in Bukhari names three mosques worth setting out on a journey to visit: this one, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem. This one is today; the other two come next. The Sacred Mosque is far from Senegal and Seattle, yet in a sense it is present in any prayer room set out to face it. The first house, still at the center.
screen: `THE SACRED, INVIOLABLE PLACE.` · `THE FIRST SANCTUARY, AT BECCA.` · `TURN THY FACE TOWARD IT.` · `THREE MOSQUES WORTH THE JOURNEY.` · then, large: `THE FIRST HOUSE.`

segments.voice: If you have a phone, open a compass or qibla app and find the direction of Mecca from where you are, or guess roughly, and turn your chair or your body that way. Notice that right now people in other rooms and other countries face the same point from every side, like spokes of a wheel. If you pray, you can pray facing it in the way you know; if not, sit facing it and let the picture of that courtyard rest in your mind.
Masjid al-Haram. The Sacred Mosque around the Ka'ba in Mecca, the direction of every Muslim prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the first house. Every qibla arrow, anywhere, points to it. See you in Medina tomorrow.

1036.title: The Prophet's Mosque
1036.hook: in Medina, built over his home and beside his grave
1036.howItsDone: Muslims visiting Medina pray in the Prophet's Mosque, hope to pray in the Rawdah between his house and his pulpit, and greet him with salutations at his resting place; everywhere else, they send salawat on him, especially in prayer and on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Masjid al-Haram, the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the direction of every prayer. Your line was the first house. Today, the second of the three.

Mud bricks. Palm trunks for pillars. Palm fronds for a roof that leaked when it rained. A man carrying bricks with the others, sleeves dusty, while they sing as they work. That man, the reports say, is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, newly arrived in Medina, building a place to pray beside the rooms where he will live. No dome. No marble. A yard, a shade, a door onto his home. Today: the Prophet's Mosque.
screen: `MUD BRICKS AND PALM TRUNKS.` → `HE CARRIES BRICKS TOO.` → `A YARD, A SHADE, A DOOR HOME.`

segments.voice: In Arabic it's al-Masjid an-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque. It began as that simple yard in Medina, and it wasn't only for prayer. It was where he taught, where visitors and envoys were received, where the poor sat in its shade, where questions were brought and disputes settled. His home opened right onto it. When he died, he was buried in his own room, the room of his wife Aisha, and over the generations the mosque grew outward until that room now lies inside it, beneath a green dome. Muslims visit Medina, often around Hajj or Umrah, to pray in the mosque and to greet him at his resting place. A hadith in Bukhari says that between his house and his pulpit lies a garden of the gardens of Paradise. That small stretch of carpet is called the Rawdah, the garden, and visitors hope to pray there. Here's what the place teaches. A great mosque now covers the spot, but its heart is a home: a man who lived among his people, ate with them, built with them, and is greeted there still. And the Qur'an gives believers a way to greet him from anywhere: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." That asking is called salawat. No one has to be in Medina to send it. His mosque is in Medina; the greeting can come from any kitchen.
screen: `A YARD THAT BECAME A MOSQUE.` · `TAUGHT, RECEIVED, SHELTERED.` · `HIS ROOM, BENEATH THE GREEN DOME.` · `ASK BLESSINGS ON HIM.` · then, large: `HIS MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Picture that first yard, palm trunks and mud walls and a man sitting with his companions in the shade, then the mosque today, the green dome, people standing quietly to greet him. If you pray, you can say the familiar words Muslims use, Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, O God, send blessings on Muhammad, softly on each out-breath. If you don't, simply hold the picture of that first yard, and the people who built it.

Rawdah, the small stretch of the Prophet's Mosque called a garden of Paradise, where visitors hope to pray. Today's word, closing a week of pilgrims' planes, radio voices, women scholars, a hurting ummah, two billion and two holy mosques.
Your line: his mosque. It began as a yard its own people built together. That's the week, and day one thousand thirty-six.
